contributions.headingText: Ductal adenoma is a benign tumour composed of distorted glands in a sclerotic stroma surrounded by a fibrous capsule.

Ductal adenoma arises in medium-sized and small ducts of the peripheral breast.

Ductal adenoma usually presents as a palpable solitary lump, but it may have an irregular appearance when multifocal. It usually arises from the small and medium-sized ducts. Rarely, it can involve the larger ducts and present with nipple discharge, similar to intraductal papilloma. Few cases of infarction have been described in pregnancy and lactation {17146162}. Imaging usually reveals a well-circumscribed lesion but may have suspicious features {32385901}. For example, mammography usually shows a discrete mass with smooth well-defined borders or, less commonly, poorly defined margins, spiculation, multilobulation, and/or irregularly shaped calcifications. Similarly, sonography usually shows a well-defined, round hypoechoic nodule, or mural nodules within cysts, with occasional reports of shadowing and posterior enhancement {25862065}. MRI shows a lobulated or oval mass with a hyperintense signal on T2-weighted imaging and inhomogeneous internal enhancement on dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI {39022161}, but rarely can show a pseudoinvasive border {25862065}.

Ductal adenoma is a rare tumour that occurs most commonly in the sixth decade of life (range: 39–83 years) {27438523}. It has been described in four cases to be bilateral and associated with Carney complex {8764753}.

Ductal adenoma predominantly arises from the small and medium-sized ductal lumina in the peripheral breast, but rarely from the larger ducts {2550351}. In contrast, intraductal papilloma arises predominantly from larger subareolar ducts but may also arise from both small and medium-sized peripheral ducts.

It is hypothesized that ductal adenoma most likely originates from intraductal papilloma in small and medium-sized ducts. Owing to a stromal repair process, intraductal papilloma may undergo sclerosis, which is manifested by a myofibroblastic proliferation and deposition of fibronectin and interstitial collagen, resulting in loss of the arborizing papillary architecture. Overlapping features of radial scar (e.g. central elastosis) may also be seen, because radial scars are considered part of the spectrum of papillary lesions. Some authors contend that a hyperplastic process such as sclerosing adenosis, which is prevalent in ductal adenoma, may lead to ductal adenoma by direct expansion into small and medium-sized ducts or into a coexistent intraductal papilloma. The few cases of ductal adenoma that have been studied using next-generation sequencing show recurrent missense mutations in PIK3CA, GNAS, and AKT1 {27438523}. AKT1 mutations have also been detected in intraductal papillomas {19898424}, supporting a close relationship with (or an origin similar to that of) ductal adenomas. The mutation pattern of ductal adenoma is different from that of tubular adenoma suggesting that these are different entities at a genomic level {27438523}.

Ductal adenomas range in size from 5 to 50 mm (average: 8.5 mm) {6090627} and present as a discrete, white, solid nodule. On cut surface, they are lobulated and granular, with central grey softening. Calcified areas may seem firm, gritty, and pseudoinvasive. Focal attachment to a dilated cyst or duct may occasionally be seen. Rarely, the tumour may have a poorly defined edge that is firmly adherent to the surrounding breast stroma, raising suspicion for an invasive carcinoma. Additionally, ductal adenoma can be multinodular owing to involvement of proximal or distal parts of the same ductal system.

Ductal adenoma is usually a solitary, solid, adenomatous proliferation surrounded by a densely thickened concentric fibroelastotic wall, but it may be multinodular at times. The adenomatous portion consists of glands arranged in organized parallel patterns, radiating outwards from the centre to the periphery. The glands range in shape from round to oval, elongated to branched, and are composed of a bilayer of luminal ductal and attenuated myoepithelial cells with a modest amount of intervening fibrous stroma. In Carney complex, the glands are tubular {8764753}. The stroma may compress and obliterate the glands, similar to in sclerosing adenosis. The glands may cystically dilate, have luminal tufting, contain PAS-positive eosinophilic secretions, and/or contain associated laminated calcifications. At high magnification, the ductal cells are noted to be cuboidal, columnar, and/or spindled, with eosinophilic cytoplasm, but they lack atypia and may have rare mitoses. The capsule is laminated and hyalinized; it contains dystrophic calcifications and thus may entrap glands or protrude into surrounding tissue and appear to have a pushing or pseudoinfiltrative border. In addition to calcifications, the sclerotic wall may also show chronic inflammation, haemorrhage, myxoid change, and squamous and chondroid metaplasia. Degenerative changes with or without calcifications may be seen in the periphery or centre; degenerative changes in the centre may resemble and overlap with histological features of a radial scar. The surrounding breast may show sclerosing adenosis, apocrine metaplasia, or cystic duct ectasia. No arborizing papillary fronds (as seen in intraductal papilloma) or myoepithelial hyperplasia (as seen in adenomyoepithelioma) is evident. By immunohistochemistry, ductal adenomas express myoepithelial markers and high-molecular-weight cytokeratins, and heterogeneously express ER, but show low p53 and Ki-67 labelling {19067857}.

As in core needle biopsy and surgical pathology the differential diagnosis includes intraductal papilloma and fibroadenoma. Highly cellular smears have been reported with plentiful cohesive 3D tissue fragments of ductal cells with myoepithelial cells and uniform nuclei with single nucleoli in a background of bare bipolar nuclei, and fragments of metachromatic (Giemsa) or eosinophilic (Pap) stroma with epithelium attached {8187593}. These stromal tufts resemble those seen in intraductal papillomas {17636490} or in some cases the globules of collagenous spherulosis.

Essential: well-circumscribed tumour composed of an adenomatous proliferation surrounded by a laminated concentric fibrosclerotic wall; round to oval, elongated to branched glands composed of a bilayer of luminal ductal and attenuated myoepithelial cells, with a modest amount of intervening fibrous stroma; cuboidal, columnar, and/or spindled ductal cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, lacking atypia, with rare mitoses.

Ductal adenoma is a benign, stable neoplasm with no increased risk for recurrence or malignancy after complete excision, a finding supported by low p53 and Ki-67 labelling {19067857}. Excision is often recommended owing to histological and radiological mimicry of carcinoma or radial scar, especially on clinical examination, imaging, and core biopsy. A few cases reported in the literature have been associated with ductal and lobular carcinoma in situ, but this association is most likely attributable to coexistence rather than malignant transformation.
